---
title: "RKI"
---

The RKI method asks a narrower question than a control chart does. Not "is this
week high?", but "is this week high *for this week of the year*?" It gathers a
handful of comparable weeks — the same week in earlier years, and the weeks just
gone — and treats what happened in them as what should happen now. It is the
instinct behind judging a June electricity bill against last June rather than
against the yearly average. Set the three parameters below and watch which weeks
get pulled into the comparison.

::: {#fig-refset}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-refset"></div>
```

Building the reference set for one week. Selected weeks are shaded; the week
under assessment is outlined.
:::

The Robert Koch Institute built this into SurvNet, Germany's national electronic
notification system, in 2001 [@faensen2006; @rki_practical]. It follows the CDC method of Stroup
and colleagues [@stroup1989], which introduced the idea of judging a week
against the equivalent weeks of earlier years rather than against one overall
average. Höhle's `surveillance` package implements it as `algo.rki`
[@hoehle2007; @hoehle_riebler_surveillance].

## Computing an epidemic threshold with RKI {#sec-rki-threshold}

For weekly case counts the tool is `algo.rki` in R's `surveillance` package,
with `algo.rki1`, `algo.rki2` and `algo.rki3` as named presets [@salmon2016]. It
runs in three steps.

::: {.algo-step}
**1. Reference set.** Collect the weeks that count as comparable to week $t$.
They come from two places: a window of width $2w+1$ centred on the equivalent
week in each of the $b$ previous years, and the $w_0$ weeks immediately before
$t$ in the current year.

$$
R_{w,w_0,b} \;=\; \left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{b}\ \bigcup_{j=-w}^{w} y_{\,t-52i+j}\right)
\;\cup\; \left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{w_0} y_{\,t-k}\right)
$$

Here $y_t$ is the number of cases notified in week $t$, and 52 is the number of
weeks the package assumes in a year.
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**2. Expected level.** Average them.

$$ \hat\mu = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{y \,\in\, R_{w,w_0,b}} y, \qquad n = \bigl|R_{w,w_0,b}\bigr|. $$

There is no fitted curve and no trend term. The reference weeks *are* the model.
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**3. Threshold.** Take the upper limit of a two-sided 95% interval for a count
of that size. `algo.rki` picks the interval two different ways, depending on how
large $\hat\mu$ is:

$$
U_t \;=\;
\begin{cases}
\hat\mu + 2\hat\sigma, & \hat\mu > 20,\\[4pt]
\tfrac{1}{2}\,\chi^2_{0.975}\bigl(2(\lfloor\hat\mu\rfloor+1)\bigr), & \hat\mu \le 20,
\end{cases}
$$

with $\hat\sigma$ the sample standard deviation of the reference values. A week
signals when $N_t > U_t$.
:::

The defaults are $b=2$, $w=4$ and `actY = FALSE` — the RKI 3 system — the
comparison is strict, so a week that exactly meets the threshold stays quiet,
and $U_t$ is never rounded to a whole case, so 24 notifications against a
threshold of 23.49 is a signal.

### How many weeks the comparison uses {#sec-rki-size}

The two sources of reference weeks never overlap, provided $w_0 < 52 - w$, so
the size of the set is just the two pieces added together. Count each one.

The current year contributes a single week for each $k$ from 1 to $w_0$:

$$ n_{\text{current}} = w_0. $$

Each past year contributes a single week for each $j$ from $-w$ to $w$, which is
$2w+1$ weeks, and there are $b$ such years:

$$ n_{\text{past}} = b\,(2w+1). $$

Add them:

$$ n = w_0 + b\,(2w+1). $$

Nothing here depends on the case counts. The **size of the comparison is fixed
by the calendar alone**, decided before any data is read, which is what makes
the three published systems directly comparable.

One implementation detail matters when you go to run it. In `algo.rki` the two
widths are not independent: the current-year window is switched on by `actY` and
reuses the same $w$, so

$$ w_0 = w \cdot \mathbf{1}\{\texttt{actY}\}, $$

and the package labels its output `rki(w, w0, b)` accordingly. A setting like
$w=1$ with $w_0=2$ is expressible in the definition above but not through
`algo.rki`; it needs a hand-rolled reference set.

### Where the two branches come from {#sec-rki-branches}

Both branches answer one question: how large can a count get before it stops
looking like a draw from the reference level?

When the expected count is large, the reference values are roughly symmetric
about their mean, and the upper limit of a two-sided 95% interval sits about two
standard deviations above it. The package rounds 1.96 to 2 and takes

$$ U_t = \hat\mu + 2\hat\sigma. $$

When the expected count is small that approximation fails: counts are discrete,
the distribution is skewed, and a symmetric interval can reach below zero. So
the package uses the exact Poisson limit instead. For an observation $x$, the
upper limit is the rate at which $x$ or fewer cases would be seen only 2.5% of
the time:

$$ \Pr\bigl(X \le x \mid \lambda = U\bigr) = 0.025, $$

which has a closed form in terms of the chi-square quantile,

$$ U = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\chi^2_{0.975}\bigl(2(x+1)\bigr). $$

`algo.rki` reads this out of a stored table (`CIdata`, tabulated by Sachs
[@sachs1991]) at $x = \lfloor\hat\mu\rfloor$, the reference mean rounded down to
a whole case. That floor is why $U_t$ is a **step function**: it holds still
while the reference mean drifts, then jumps the moment the mean crosses an
integer.

A quicker approximation is sometimes quoted for this step, $\hat\mu +
1.96\sqrt{\hat\mu}$, which treats the reference mean as a Poisson rate. It lands
close, but it is not what the package computes, and it is the more permissive of
the two — on the example below it gives 23.16 where the table gives 24.74.

### The example in @fig-refset {#sec-rki-example}

The figure opens on a worked case. Week 25 of 2026 is assessed with $b=3$, $w=1$
and $w_0=2$, so the reference set is the three weeks around week 25 in each of
2025, 2024 and 2023, plus weeks 23 and 24 of 2026 — eleven weeks in all, from
the formula $n = 2 + 3(2\cdot 1 + 1) = 11$. They average 15.45 cases. That is
below 20, so the Poisson branch applies: $\lfloor 15.45 \rfloor = 15$, and the
table gives $U = 24.74$. Twenty-one notifications would pass; twenty-six would
signal.

Raising $w_0$ pulls more of the current year into the comparison, and lowering
it pushes the method back onto earlier years. That single trade is what
separates the three published systems.

## RKI 1, RKI 2 and RKI 3 {#sec-rki-variants}

::: {.algo-step}
**RKI 1** — $b=0$, $w=6$, `actY = TRUE`, six reference weeks. The six weeks just
gone, and nothing else. It has no memory of previous years, so it cannot know
what time of year it is; what it can do is react within six weeks of a change.
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**RKI 2** — $b=1$, $w=6$, `actY = TRUE`, nineteen reference weeks. The same six
recent weeks, plus the thirteen weeks centred on the equivalent week one year
ago. Roughly half recent, half seasonal.
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**RKI 3** — $b=2$, $w=4$, `actY = FALSE`, eighteen reference weeks. The current
year is dropped entirely; nine weeks are taken around the equivalent week in
each of the two previous years. Every reference week is seasonal.
:::

::: {#fig-series}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-series"></div>
```

The same simulated series under all three systems. Hover a week to see the
reference weeks behind it.
:::

The consequence is visible in @fig-series. Because RKI 1 and RKI 2 include the
weeks immediately before $t$, a rise that lasts more than a few weeks **enters
its own reference set** and lifts its own threshold behind it. The simulated
rise in the fourth year of the figure spans weeks 14 to 25 of 2025: RKI 1 flags
two of those weeks, RKI 2 flags four, and RKI 3 — which never looks at the
current year — flags six.

That is not a ranking. It is a trade, and it runs in both directions. RKI 3
keeps a baseline no ongoing outbreak can inflate, but it cannot report at all
until two full years of history exist behind it; in the figure it stays silent
until week 5 of 2024, while RKI 1 is running by week 7 of 2022. A short memory
buys speed and a short warm-up and pays for it in seasonal blindness. A long one
buys a seasonal baseline and pays for it in start-up time and in slower
recognition that the baseline itself has shifted.

The series in @fig-series is simulated, not observed. It is there to show how
the threshold behaves, not how dengue behaves.

## Poisson or negative binomial {#sec-rki-dispersion}

Every threshold so far has assumed that a week's count varies about as
much as its own average. That is what lets $\sqrt{\hat\mu}$ carry the
whole of step 3: Poisson counts have variance equal to their mean, so
the mean alone fixes the spread, and no separate variance has to be
estimated.

The choice between the two distributions is not a choice about which
disease you are watching. It comes down to one question about the
reference weeks: do they vary more than their own mean?

Poisson says no. It holds when cases arrive independently, at a rate
that does not move across the reference weeks. Three things break that,
and any one is enough:

-   **Cases are not independent.** One case produces others, so they
    arrive in lumps rather than one at a time.
-   **The rate itself moves.** Whatever drives transmission changes
    across the reference weeks, so they are not draws from a single
    distribution.
-   **Reporting is uneven.** A delayed week followed by a double week
    adds variance that has nothing to do with transmission.

All three inflate the variance and leave the mean alone — the one
failure Poisson cannot express, because it has no parameter for it.

### What it costs to get this wrong {#sec-rki-inflation}

Write the excess as a dispersion factor
$\varphi = \operatorname{Var}(y) /
\operatorname{E}(y)$, so $\varphi = 1$ under Poisson. A negative
binomial with mean $\mu$ and dispersion $\varphi$ has variance
$\varphi\mu$, so its standard deviation is

$$ \sqrt{\varphi\mu} \;=\; \sqrt{\varphi}\,\sqrt{\mu}. $$

The distance from the mean up to any quantile is a multiple of the
standard deviation, so it widens by $\sqrt{\varphi}$, not by $\varphi$.
Doubling the variance moves the threshold out by about 41%.

Small in the threshold, large in the alarm rate. The `algo.rki` Poisson
branch starts out conservative — a confidence limit read from a table,
not a predictive quantile — so on true Poisson counts it fires on about
one normal week in a hundred, not the one in twenty its 95% label
suggests. Hold that threshold fixed and let the counts be overdispersed:

| Reference mean $\hat\mu$ | Threshold $U_t$ | Poisson | $\varphi = 2$ | $\varphi = 3$ | $\varphi = 5$ |
|-----------:|-----------:|-----------:|-----------:|-----------:|-----------:|
|                        5 |           11.67 |    0.6% |          3.8% |          6.7% |         10.2% |
|                       10 |           18.39 |    0.7% |          4.4% |          7.6% |         11.7% |
|                       15 |           24.74 |    1.1% |          5.4% |          9.0% |         13.4% |
|                       20 |           30.89 |    1.4% |          6.0% |          9.7% |         14.4% |

: Chance that one ordinary week trips the alarm, holding the RKI
threshold fixed and varying only the dispersion of the counts underneath
it. {#tbl-rki-dispersion}

At $\varphi = 3$, a threshold meant to fire on about 1% of normal weeks
fires on 9%: a false alarm every eleven weeks in place of one every two
years. In cases, the worked example's threshold of 24.74 would have to
sit at 33.

The error runs one way only. Assuming Poisson when $\varphi > 1$ costs
specificity, never sensitivity.

### Choosing {#sec-rki-phi}

$\varphi$ is estimated, not assumed. Estimate it from a long stretch of
non-epidemic weeks — **not** from the reference set, whose 18 or 19
values are far too few. The usual estimator is the Pearson dispersion of
a quasi-Poisson fit with the seasonality left in:

``` r
fit <- glm(cases ~ t + sin(2*pi*week/52) + cos(2*pi*week/52),
           family = quasipoisson, data = baseline)
summary(fit)$dispersion
```

**Near 1, stay with Poisson.** `algo.rki` works as it stands, needs no
second estimate, and a badly fitted dispersion is its own source of
error.

**Above about 2, move to the negative binomial.** @tbl-rki-dispersion
applies, and the Poisson threshold is delivering several times the alarm
rate it claims.

**In between, prefer Poisson when the baseline is short.** A
$\hat\varphi$ drawn from two years of weekly data is itself uncertain,
and over-estimating it raises the threshold and hides outbreaks Poisson
would have caught.

`algo.rki` has no negative binomial option. The smallest change keeps
its reference set and replaces only the last step: a negative binomial
with mean $\hat\mu$ and variance $\hat\varphi\hat\mu$ has size parameter
$k = \hat\mu / (\hat\varphi - 1)$, so

``` r
U <- qnbinom(1 - alpha, mu = mu_hat, size = mu_hat / (phi_hat - 1))
```

The reference weeks, the calendar and the decision rule are unchanged;
only the tail is. Beyond that, `farringtonFlexible` estimates dispersion
as part of fitting and downweights past outbreaks so they cannot inflate
the baseline [@farrington1996; @noufaily2013], and `boda` fits a
negative binomial outright [@salmon2016] — both at far more computation
than RKI.
